lesson.title: Many Symbols, One Idea: Notating the Second Derivative
lesson.summary: Mathematicians write the second derivative several different ways, f''(x), y'', and d^2y/dx^2 among them, and all of them refer to the exact same object: the derivative of the derivative.
lesson.body:
Calculus grew out of two independent traditions, one led by Isaac Newton and one by Gottfried Leibniz, and later contributors added their own shorthand on top. As a result, the second derivative, the rate of change of the rate of change, has more than one accepted way to write it. None of these notations is more correct than another; each is convenient in a different setting, and reading calculus fluently means recognizing all of them as the same underlying idea.

In Lagrange (prime) notation, the second derivative of f is written f''(x), read f double prime of x. If the dependent variable is named y instead of f(x), the same quantity is written y''. In Leibniz notation, it's written d^2y/dx^2, built by applying the operator d/dx twice (the next two chapters look closely at f''(x) and d^2y/dx^2 individually). You may also encounter operator notation, D^2f or D_x^2[y], mostly in more theoretical or engineering contexts, and in physics, when the independent variable is time, a second derivative is sometimes written with two dots over the variable.

Let y = x^3 - 2x. Differentiating once: y' = 3x^2 - 2. Differentiating again: y'' = 6x. This single result, 6x, can be written in any of the equivalent forms: f''(x) = 6x, y'' = 6x, or d^2y/dx^2 = 6x. Evaluated at x = 3, every one of these notations gives the same number: 18. Whichever symbol a textbook or a colleague uses, they are describing the identical fact about the curve.

Because Lagrange and Leibniz notation are the two you'll meet constantly, the next two chapters take each one in turn: how to read and use f''(x), and how to read and use d^2y/dx^2, including why that Leibniz form is not literally dy/dx squared, a common point of confusion worth clearing up carefully.
